lessons.name: Determine multiple themes of short stories

textContent.text: Nolan listened carefully to his manager, who was demonstrating how to ring up orders at the register. The two other new hires were standing a few feet away, playing with their magnetic name tags and coiling the strings from their aprons around their hands. Nolan leaned closer to the screen; he wanted to get every step right.

Mr. Marković noticed that Nolan seemed to be the only one paying attention, so he let him take the first practice order. Nolan's fingers fumbled on the touch screen, and he accidentally hit "burger" instead of "milkshake," but Mr. Marković patiently showed him how to remove his selections and try again.
"If a customer changes their mind, do I hit 'void' here or go back a step?" Nolan asked.
"Back a step," the manager replied, impressed by the question. "That way, the register keeps track of what you corrected."

Nolan's attention to detail impressed Mr. Marković, who decided he could be trusted to work the register for his first shift, while the other two new hires would sweat it out at the grill. Nolan sighed in relief—everyone knew the register was the best assignment.

Over the next week, Nolan continued working at the register but also bagged orders, ran the drive-thru, and even unloaded the food delivery trucks. On Friday night, when he clocked out and slung his apron over his shoulder, Mr. Marković called him into the break room.
"Nice work, Nolan. You've really done a great job," he said, handing him an envelope.

Nolan waited until he was outside to open it, and when he saw his very first paycheck, he whooped with excitement. He thought of the late nights, the difficult customers, and the smell of grease in his work clothes. In that moment, he felt like all those hours on his feet had paid off. Already, he was doing the math, counting how many more paychecks it might take to buy a car.

textContent.text: Makai put in his earbuds and began shelving tubs of yogurt while humming along to the music. He lifted the cartons onto the shelves and shoved them toward the glass doors that faced the shoppers. He grinned and waved as a woman reaching for a tub of vanilla jumped at the sight of him; customers were always surprised that people worked in the walk-in cooler behind the dairy shelves.

pieces.text: When he finished restocking the yogurt, he heard a truck pull up to the loading dock.
, he thought—

content.text: that would be Leslie with the milk delivery.

pieces.text: He grabbed a hand truck and headed out back to help.

textContent.text: Eager to keep up with Leslie so she wouldn't be late to her next stop, Makai stacked the milk crates six high, just above the top of his head, but on his third trip, he took a corner too quickly and lost control. The stack wobbled, then crashed down, gallons bursting and flowing swiftly across the concrete. Makai's stomach sank as milk pooled around his boots.

pieces.text: For a moment, he considered finding something to blame.

content.text: Maybe there was a loose wheel

pieces.text: , he thought,

content.text: a wet patch of floor, a box left in the way, anything!

pieces.text: But Makai's conscience tugged at him. Taking a deep breath, he found his manager, Mr. Larsen, and confessed: "I rushed and dropped a bunch of milk crates. It's a mess, and it's my fault."

textContent.text: At first, Mr. Larsen's expression was stern, but seeing that Makai was earnest, he softened. "Thanks for owning up to it, Makai. I'll help you with the cleanup."

The two grabbed mops and buckets, tackling the sticky chaos. Mr. Larsen shared a story of the time he accidentally collapsed an entire shelf of cottage cheese, and Makai laughed, his embarrassment fading. After a few minutes of work, the floor was once again gleaming. Mr. Larsen patted Makai's shoulder, thanked him again for telling him what happened, and told him what a good job he was doing.

textContent.text: On his first day at Willow Creek Middle School, AJ sat at the end of a long, empty table, pretending to study his sandwich like there was something interesting about it. All around him, the cafeteria buzzed with chatter, but AJ shrank into his seat. He slid in his earbuds and buried his eyes in his phone.

A couple of tables away, Ethan set his tray down next to his two best friends, who were complaining about the quiz they had just taken in history. Ethan tried to listen and even muttered a vague, sympathetic "hmm," but he was distracted. He kept glancing at AJ, sitting alone, bouncing gently to the beat in his headphones. Ethan didn't know him, but the sight of AJ alone left him shifting uneasily in his seat.
Finally, Ethan pushed back his chair and walked over to sit across from AJ. "What's on your playlist?" he asked.
Surprised, AJ took out his right earbud. "What?"
"Your playlist," Ethan said. "What's on it?"

After a pause, AJ slowly turned his phone toward Ethan so he could see the screen. Ethan scrolled through the list, a look of appreciation spreading across his face. "No way!" he exclaimed, breaking out into a huge grin. "You like Neon Avalanche, too?" Ethan then launched into a story about the first time he heard their new album and how it literally changed his life.

AJ smiled, relaxing for the first time that day. For the rest of lunch, the two boys shared favorite songs and debated the best bands, their laughter drawing the attention of Ethan's friends, who came to join them.

Headed to his next class, this time flanked by Ethan and his friends, AJ felt lighter than he had all day. He had really enjoyed lunch and—even better—no longer felt invisible. He smiled as he realized he might actually like his new school.

textContent.text: Tegan's fingers tripped over the flute keys as she fumbled through the fast notes, the melody dissolving into just noise. She lowered her head and groaned. After playing for two years, practicing almost every day, she still couldn't make it through the quick runs. Tegan felt stuck.
Her thoughts drifted to band class earlier that week, when Mr. Alvarez had asked her to help Lila, a beginner. At the time, Tegan had agreed, but now she wondered if she was the right person to help.

A knock on the practice room door startled Tegan. Lila stepped inside, clutching her flute case like it might slip from her hands. "Hi," Lila said, her voice a little breathless. "Thank you for helping me—I can't get anything to sound right." She laughed nervously.
"Me neither," Tegan muttered, then flushed. "I mean—I still make mistakes all the time."
Lila's eyes widened. "Are you kidding? You sound amazing. I wish I could play like you," she said as she sat down and began assembling her flute.
The compliment caught Tegan off guard. She had only ever focused on her squeaks and stumbles; it was difficult to imagine that someone else heard only the music.
Tegan lifted her flute, demonstrated a simple scale, and watched Lila copy her fingering.

Their first practice session was clumsy—false starts and nervous giggles—but somewhere along the way, between explaining how to fully cover the holes and how to steady a breath, Tegan began to look at her own playing differently. She realized where her own fingers sometimes slipped and how her own breath wasn't always steady.

Over the next few weeks, the girls met twice a week, and Lila slowly improved. Tegan also noticed that her own playing benefited from helping Lila. She was able to polish the rough spots she had overlooked. For the first time in months, she felt like she was moving forward, and maybe, just maybe, she wasn't as bad as she had thought.

textContent.text: Selena stared at the caution tape and orange cones blocking the entrance to the bike lane. She knew it was temporary, but somehow a year-long project didn't feel very temporary to her. With a final sigh, she grasped her handlebars and turned away from the bridge.

For two years, Selena had ridden her bike to school, crossing under the bridge that was just blocks from her house. Over the summer, however, the city closed the bridge for repairs, so she and her dad had practiced a few different detours. They eventually decided that the greenway, a tree-lined path that stretched alongside the river, would be the easiest, though it turned Selena's five-minute bike ride into at least a fifteen-minute trip.

Selena pedaled on the bumpy pavement, distracted by all the unfamiliar sounds—birds chirping, leaves rustling, the steady rush of the river—that had replaced the familiar, hollow rumble of cars rolling over the bridge. She sped up, missing her old shortcut, though at least the big trees and splashing water gave her something pretty to look at.

Nearing a fork in the trail, she spotted a girl from her school pedaling toward her from the other path. They hadn't ever talked, but they knew each other in that awkward way of kids who share a school building but not much else. Selena stopped, setting her feet on the pavement and holding one handlebar; the other rider stopped, too.
"Hey," she said.
"Hey," Selena responded. "Guess you're going to school, too?"
The girl, whose name was Annie, nodded. "I've never seen you out here before," she said, curiously.
"Yeah, well—the bridge," Selena said, tipping her head back toward the crane that loomed over the construction zone.
"Oh, right," Annie murmured, glancing down. "Maybe we could ride together?"

Selena agreed quickly, and they began to ride again, this time side by side. Selena and Annie began to talk about their favorite bike routes around town, and Annie pointed out a forking path off the greenway that climbed a steep hill. "My brother says that path leads to the new ice cream shop, but I've never been," she said. "Maybe we can ride there together sometime?"
Selena smiled: The ride with Annie suddenly felt less like a tiresome detour and more like a new adventure.

textContent.text: Jurnee laced up her sneakers and grabbed her water bottle before shoving her book bag into the locker. Normally, she enjoyed school, but today was different. Today was the timed mile run in gym class, and the thought of it made her stomach twist.

She had done okay in gym before—passing the sit-up test, clearing the jump-rope challenge, even making a layup now and then. Distance running, though, felt like a different beast. A mile seemed endless, like climbing a mountain. Over and over, she pictured herself gasping for air, tripping over her own feet, or worse—giving up in front of everyone.
Addie slid into the bench next to her. "You good?"
Jurnee sighed. "The mile's today."
Addie placed a reassuring hand on her shoulder. "Just breathe. I'll run with you—every step."
Jurnee blinked. "But you run cross country."
"Forget that. What matters is I'm sticking with you from start to finish."
Jurnee gave her friend a half-smile and mumbled her appreciation.

By the time they reached the track, the rest of the class was already gathering at the starting line. When their teacher blew the whistle, Jurnee took off at a medium pace. Her legs felt heavy almost immediately, every step a reminder of how far she still had to go.
Then Jurnee became aware of footsteps beside her. Turning her head, she saw Addie, keeping pace—calm and unhurried. For the first time that day, Jurnee felt her doubts begin to loosen their grip.

With each lap, Jurnee's anxiety faded while her confidence grew. When they rounded the final turn, her legs ached and her lungs burned, but something inside her had shifted. She quickened her pace, pouring every ounce of energy she had left into the last few yards.
"Hey!" called Addie, who laughed and sped up to join her.
Crossing the finish line, Jurnee doubled over, breathless. "I didn't think I could do it." She straightened, then wrapped her arms around Addie, overwhelmed with gratitude.

Jurnee gave her friend a half-smile and mumbled her appreciation.

"Hey!" called Addie, who laughed and sped up to join her.
Crossing the finish line, Jurnee doubled over, breathless. "I didn't think I could do it." She straightened, then wrapped her arms around Addie, overwhelmed with gratitude.

textContent.text: Priya looked around the empty gym and breathed in. As student council president, she was in charge of decorating for the dance and had spent weeks ordering materials to go with her "retro arcade" theme. She had thought of everything: neon streamers, black lights, cardboard cutouts, even a balloon arch to provide a grand entrance. But what she hadn't thought about was setting everything up. She looked at the small mountain of unopened boxes stacked at center court and let out the breath she hadn't realized she'd been holding.
"Priya! Where is your decorating crew?" Mrs. Jenkins asked.
Priya jumped a little—she hadn't heard the principal come in. "I prefer to work alone," she answered.
"Do you want me to grab some helpers for you?"
"No—I'll be okay," Priya said, nodding to reassure herself as much as Mrs. Jenkins.
The principal raised her eyebrows but told Priya to let her know if she needed anything, then left.

An hour later, Priya had barely made a dent. Streamers snaked across the floor; balloons rolled lazily into the corners. Clenching her fists, she let out a low groan and headed toward Mrs. Jenkins's office.

Mrs. Jenkins smiled when she saw Priya and immediately picked up her phone and made an announcement over the PA system. Within minutes, a steady stream of students was headed for the gym, and Priya felt a weight being lifted from her shoulders.

Priya showed her floor plan to the group, who listened, then got to work. It was a big job, but she was amazed by how quickly things came together—one group hung streamers while another set up black lights along the walls. Four kids tied clusters of balloons together, creating a brightly colored archway. Several others assembled the cardboard cutouts of arcade cabinets and 8-bit characters. Soon, the gym became a glowing arcade world, and Priya beamed with pride and gratitude for everyone who had come to her rescue.

textContent.text: Darius carefully reviewed the list, then scanned it again, but he didn't see his number anywhere. As some of the other boys high-fived, celebrating their spots on the baseball team, Darius slung his backpack over one shoulder, tugged the bill of his cap low, and slipped out the side door of the locker room.

Baseball had been part of his life for as long as he could remember, starting Little League when he was seven and making his middle school team all three years. He might have sat the bench more than he played, but Darius was always early to practice and frequently stayed late to help the coach. Darius trudged home, the sting of rejection still sharp inside him.
Later that evening, his phone buzzed with a new email; it was from Coach Ramirez.

pieces.text: , the message began.

content.text: I know you didn't make the roster, but I'd like to offer you a spot as our practice catcher. At practices, you'd be helping our pitchers get their work in, and at games, you'd help warm them up. I know it's not the same as playing, but it's an important job, and I think you'd be good at it.

textContent.text: Darius's stomach sank. Practice catcher? Did that even count as being on the team? He closed the email without answering.

But later, lying in bed, he couldn't stop thinking about the weight of the catcher's gear, the snap of the ball hitting the leather glove, the rhythm of signal, windup, and throw. Who was he kidding? Baseball meant too much to him to quit now. It didn't matter that he wouldn't be on the roster—at least he'd still be helping the team. He opened the email again, and this time he hit reply.
As the message whooshed away, Darius felt his disappointment fade. He was already picturing what it would be like getting fitted for his catcher's gear and learning all the new pitching signs.

textContent.text: Nolan listened carefully to his manager, who was demonstrating how to ring up orders at the register. The two other new hires were standing a few feet away, playing with their magnetic name tags and coiling the strings from their aprons around their hands. Nolan leaned closer to the screen; he wanted to get every step right.

Mr. Marković noticed that Nolan seemed to be the only one paying attention, so he let him take the first practice order. Nolan's fingers fumbled on the touch screen, and he accidentally hit "burger" instead of "milkshake," but Mr. Marković patiently showed him how to remove his selections and try again.
"If a customer changes their mind, do I hit 'void' here or go back a step?" Nolan asked.
"Back a step," the manager replied, impressed by the question. "That way, the register keeps track of what you corrected."

Nolan's attention to detail impressed Mr. Marković, who decided he could be trusted to work the register for his first shift, while the other two new hires would sweat it out at the grill. Nolan sighed in relief—everyone knew the register was the best assignment.

Over the next week, Nolan continued working at the register but also bagged orders, ran the drive-thru, and even unloaded the food delivery trucks. On Friday night, when he clocked out and slung his apron over his shoulder, Mr. Marković called him into the break room.
"Nice work, Nolan. You've really done a great job," he said, handing him an envelope.

Nolan waited until he was outside to open it, and when he saw his very first paycheck, he whooped with excitement. He thought of the late nights, the difficult customers, and the smell of grease in his work clothes. In that moment, he felt like all those hours on his feet had paid off. Already, he was doing the math, counting how many more paychecks it might take to buy a car.

header.text: A root is a part of a word that has a certain meaning. Words that share the same root often have similar meanings that are related to the meaning of the root. For example:

contents.text: The root phon means sound.

sentences.text: A xylophone is a musical instrument with wooden bars that are hit by small hammers.

A telephone is a machine that can carry the sound of someone's voice over a long distance.

contents.text: All of these meanings relate to the concept of sound.

contents.text: Use quotation marks around a direct quotation from a speaker or a written source. A direct quotation can be written in several ways.

header.text: The quotation can come after the speaker tag.

sentences.text: The speaker declared, "We can succeed by working together."
He demanded, "Who's there?"
Use a comma to separate the speaker tag from the quotation, and capitalize the first word of the quotation.

header.text: The quotation can come before the speaker tag.

sentences.text: "We can succeed by working together," the speaker declared.
"Who's there?" he demanded.

Unless the quotation ends with a question mark or exclamation point, separate it from the speaker tag with a comma. Do not capitalize the speaker tag unless it begins with a proper noun or the pronoun I.

header.text: The quotation can be interrupted by the speaker tag.

sentences.text: "We can succeed," the speaker declared, "by working together."
Use commas to separate the speaker tag from the quotation. Do not capitalize the second part of the quotation.

header.text: Commas and periods always go inside closing quotation marks. Question marks and exclamation points should go inside only when they are part of the quotation.

sentences.text: "Who's there?" he demanded.
He demanded, "Who's there?"
